idiom_name: parent struct owns the shared state; children take a pointer and register themselves
implementation_notes: C has no component tree, no ambient scope and no closures, so the pattern is the hand-written structure: the parent is a struct that owns the shared value plus a table of registered children (pointers to child structs, each carrying its own callback), and every child constructor takes the parent pointer and registers itself. What replaces the classic structure is that explicit registration plus a callback per child; a toolkit-supplied group object is preferable whenever the UI framework already owns the grouping semantics, because re-implementing it invites disagreement with the toolkit's focus and rendering rules. Because nothing re-renders automatically, the parent must also drive the redraw after a child reports a change - in C the pattern is mostly an ownership and invariant arrangement, not an API sugar.
pitfalls: No ownership story: without an explicit teardown the parent's child table dangles after the children are freed (use one arena or a documented destroy order).
Registration is manual and unordered - a child added twice or after the parent's render pass is silently ignored unless you assert on capacity and duplicates.
Nothing re-renders automatically: the parent must be told to repaint after an update, otherwise the UI keeps showing the previous selection.
Because children hold a pointer to the parent, a child outliving its parent is a use-after-free; state the lifetime rule in the header.
